title: The Surangama Sutra (Class Part 3)
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart and IkuShun Desiree Webster
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart and IkuShun Desiree Webster take up part four of the Surangama Sutra in the third class of their series. IkuShun reads the Buddha's account of how the world of illusion arises from adding understanding to understanding, and the parable of Yajnadatta, who runs madly from home after he loses his face in a mirror. IkuShun also tells of looking through a microscope with a young son and feeling more care for the creatures from the planter than for the blood cells. Kanho plays a gorilla video to show change blindness, then turns to Ananda's reliance on his senses and the Buddha's bell test, where the sound ends while hearing goes on.

**IkuShun Desiree Webster:** Thanks for remembering.
Here we are again, ready to venture into the wonderful world of Surangama.
Tonight I'm going to start with part four, which is called the coming into being of the world of illusion.
There are four chapters in this.
Chapter one is called adding understanding to understanding.
In this part of the Surangama Sutra, we explore true reality and becoming lost in the maze of illusion.
We begin as Purnamaitriyaniputra, a senior disciple, poses questions.

If the primary elements are illusory in the form we experience them, while nevertheless being fundamentally identical to the matrix of the thus come one, how is it that they come into being as separate illusory entities?
The Buddha explains that everything flows from our initial error of dividing reality into self and other.

This process begins with what the Buddha calls adding understanding to understanding, and leads to a division of what was originally a unified awareness into an observer who is separate from what is observed.
So let's begin.
*Purnamaitriyaniputra, addressed the world honored one.

If in fact the aggregates, the faculties, the various perceived objects and the consciousnesses of all of the matrix of the thus come one, which is itself fundamentally pure, then how is it that suddenly there came into being the mountains, the rivers and all else on Earth that exists subject to conditions?
And why are all of these subject to a succession of changes, ending and beginning again?

The thus come one also said that everywhere throughout the Dharma realm,* I like that word, we're going to talk about that more in a little while, *the primary elements, earth, water, fire and wind, are in their fundamental nature completely infused with each other, tranquil and everlasting.
World honored one, if the primary element earth extended everywhere throughout the Dharma realm, how could it coexist with water?
And if the primary element water extended everywhere throughout the Dharma realm, the primary element fire could not come into being.
How may we understand that primary elements water and fire can both pervade empty space without overcoming each other in mutual annihilation?
World honored one, the nature of the primary element earth is that it's solid, while the primary element space is that it is transparent and void.
How could they both exist everywhere throughout the Dharma realm?*
I am not sure how I understand the implications of this concept.

*The world honored one said to Purna and to all the other arhats in the assembly who were free from outflows and needed no further instruction,* I thought that was kind of interesting that that's in there, because I'm thinking again that a lot of the people are there just to support Ananda in this confusion.
Otherwise that little sentence wouldn't be in there.

But anyway: *the arhats who were free from outflows and needed no further instruction, today, for the sake of everyone in the assembly, the thus come one will explain the most supreme truth among supreme truths, so that all hearers of the teaching in this assembly who have no further aspirations, all of you arhats who have not yet experienced the two kinds of emptiness,* which are, people are empty of any real permanent self or soul, and phenomena are empty of any real and permanent essential attributes, *but have turned towards the great vehicle, as well as others, may enter the true Aranya,* a quiet place in the forest, *the state of genuine practice that will lead you to become Buddhas.
Listen carefully as I explain.
Purna, you have asked me why the mountains, the rivers and everything else on this great earth have come into being from the matrix of the thus come one, which is fundamentally pure.
Now, have you not heard that the thus come one speaks of wondrous understanding, which is intrinsic to our inherent enlightenment, to our fundamental wondrous luminous understanding?*
*Purna replied, yes, world honored one.

The Buddha said, when we talk about this understanding which characterizes enlightenment, do we mean an understanding that is intrinsic to our inherited enlightened nature, or does this inherent enlightenment lack understanding until we gain it when enlightenment is realized?
Purna said, our enlightenment is characterized by understanding only when that understanding is added to it.
Is that right or not?
The Buddha said, suppose as you say that for our inherent enlightenment to be characterized by understanding, that understanding must be added to it when enlightenment is realized.
But an enlightenment to which an understanding is added cannot be a true enlightenment.

Such an enlightenment would indeed lack understanding if understanding were not added, but an enlightenment that lacks understanding cannot be a true intrinsic enlightenment that is inherently pure and endowed with understanding.
Therefore, if you think that an understanding must be added to your inherent enlightenment, you are falsifying the true understanding, the great enlightenment.*
So I added this commentary from Hsuan Hua:
*Enlightenment is not something that requires the addition of understanding, because understanding is already inherent in enlightenment.
Once an understanding is added, an object is established.
This is the first of the three subtle aspects of delusion.
Once an object is falsely set up, you as a false subject come into being as a reaction to the false object.
This is the source of your deluded thinking.
In this way subjectivity is created.
This ultimately unreal process is the second subtle aspect of delusion, the aspect of evolving.
The general import of the section of text is that basically we are all Buddhas.
Then if we originally were Buddhas, how do we become ordinary living beings?
And why haven't ordinary beings become Buddhas?
Where does the problem lie?
Originally we were no different from Buddhas, but living beings can be created from within the Buddha nature.
The Buddha nature is radiant.
It is our fundamental enlightenment, and it is the wondrous light of enlightenment inherent in all of us.
It is from this light that beings are created.*
One of the analogies is we can say that fundamental enlightenment is a light that's already on.
If you flip the switch, you have just added something extra, and in the process you have just now turned off the light.
I kind of like that one.
The next section here, the Buddha goes on and it's very explicit and very detailed, and I didn't put all of it in there.
So you can read it if you want to.
It's really interesting.
It just goes into very minute detail about how we're all created and how all of this karma, which is not so good karma, perpetuates everything.

But we know that we have good karma too, although we have to really look at that, because even within our good karma there may be little pieces, hidden agendas that still have a little bit to do with our ego.
But anyway, I'll read this part.
*The Buddha goes on to say that the turmoil of this mutual complementarity gives rise to mental strain.
And as the mental strain is prolonged, grasping at objects of the mind begins.
Mental strain and grasping at objects together create a turbidity of mind in which afflictions are generated.
Motion becomes the world of perceived objects and stillness is distinguished as space.
In addition to space, which is undifferentiated, the world, which is differentiated, are combined, are conditioned phenomena that are neither differentiated nor the same.*

In this chapter, the Buddha goes on to talk very explicitly about how all conditioned things arise because of emotion, mental activity, union, and separation, causing beings to shift from one form to another.
He says they ascend or fall entirely in accord with their karma.
These are the causes and conditions for the perpetuation of beings.
I won't get into details word for word with this.
But the Buddha states that because of excessive desire and emotional love, all crave nourishment, a craving which will not cease.
And the world's beings devour one another and are in turn devoured.
I just think of, everything eats.
But anyway, the way he describes this is kind of hard to take.
*They devour each other and are in turn devoured according to the measure of strength or weakness.
The root of all of this becomes a desire to kill and continues the cycle of death and rebirth.*
I was thinking, ooh.
But then I guess in a way all beings, or at least carnivores, have a desire to kill.
But all things eat, it's just really interesting to me.
Anyway:
*This evil karma of the mutual devouring accompanies each of these beings.
And the root of all this is the urge to steal.
Suppose you are in debt to someone for having taken his life.
He will want to take your life in repayment.
Due to such causes and conditions, beings must pass through hundreds of thousands of eons in an everlasting succession of deaths and rebirths.
The root of all this is killing, stealing and emotional love.*
I kind of think of these things as they relate also to our precepts class.
*Those three and nothing else are the causes and conditions for the perpetuation of retribution in accord with karma.
Perna, these three distorted...*
Sorry, I can't talk tonight.
*Perpetuations ultimately derive from adding an understanding to understanding, inherent enlightenment.
From this added understanding, a false understanding arises.
From that, a deluded awareness brings into being the mountains, the rivers and all of the other conditioned phenomena in the world.
Due to that illusory awareness, we experience the world as constantly changing patterns, which are perpetually coming into our awareness and then disappearing.*
I wanted to add a little note here.
I was thinking about this this morning.
Right now I'm in an intensive with Shohaku Okumura on the teachings of Menzan, who was a teacher in the lineage of Dogen.
Menzan explained the following image from the Avatamsaka Sutra.
It says, no need for mental struggle and there is no waste of energy, meaning not to add the thinking and discrimination of sentient consciousness to true reality.
To me, that was another way of saying not to add understanding on top of understanding.
Chapter two is a short one, I think.
The Buddha's awareness is irreversible.

*Perna then asked, if our wondrous enlightenment is fundamentally wondrous, awake and endowed with luminous understanding, and if the mind of the thus come one neither increases nor diminishes, how is it then that all beings and all conditioned phenomena, the mountains, the rivers and everything on earth, suddenly arise without a reason?

Also, now that the thus come one has realized wondrous emptiness and understanding, will the mountains and rivers and all the conditioned phenomena, as well as habits and outflows of beings, ever arise in him again?*
*The Buddha said to Perna, consider the analogy of someone who loses his way in a village and becomes confused about which way is north and which way is south.
Has he mistaken his directions because of confusion or because of understanding?
Perna replied, he is lost neither because of confusion nor because of understanding.
Confusion has no basis in reality, and so how could it be the cause of his being lost?
As for understanding, how could that be the cause of his being lost?

The Buddha said, suppose this confused person who has become lost in the village unexpectedly meets someone who knows which direction is which and who points out the way to him so that he understands.
What do you think, Perna?
He's lost in the village, but now will he become lost again?
He will not, world-honored one.
The same is true, Perna, of the thus come ones throughout the ten directions.
Confusion has no basis in reality.
In its very nature, it is ultimately empty.
There was never anything real about confusion.
It only seems that there has been confusion and understanding.
Once one has awakened from one's confusion, the confusion disappears, and from that awakening, no confusion can arise again.*
Now I want to start into chapter three, which is called the interfusing of primary elements.
But before I do that, I wanted to just recap a little bit in the previous part, the matrix of the thus come one.
I felt like there was this really important point about the primary elements that, I'll read it.
An important point about the primary elements was that they were all identical to the real nature of emptiness, that includes water, air, fire, et cetera.
And these elements are fundamentally pure and extend throughout the Dharma realm.
The extent to which beings are aware of that depends on their capacity for understanding.
Then the Buddha gave examples of these elements.

For instance, when discussing wind, just as a puff of wind arises from a small movement of your robe, so a puff of wind could arise anywhere throughout the Dharma realm, in any land, when somebody moves their robe.
Since wind can arise anywhere in the world, how could it be limited to one particular place?
The Buddha says that the primary elements become apparent to beings in accord with their karma.

And he also says ordinary beings in their ignorance mistakenly suppose that the primary elements, for instance wind, come into being from causes and conditions, or that they come into being on their own.
So these distinctions and constructs are made by the conscious mind.

Robert Rosenbaum, in the other book, *This Is Not Your Mind*, with the commentaries, explains it like this: *The Buddha then shows how each thing does not come into being from causes and conditions, nor does it come into being on its own.* In the commentary, Robert states that *the Buddha employs a series of logical arguments to demonstrate that while the objects we experience are dependent on causes and conditions, they do not arise from causes and conditions.* When I read all of these, there were all these little things about the wind and about the water.
He gave an example of each one and then said that these don't arise from causes and conditions, nor do they arise on their own.
I remember reading that with Peter and Toy and I was like, "Wait a minute, what?"
I was confused because in my mind I had always learned that things arise, that things come into being from causes and conditions.
So that was confusing to me, and I kept wrestling with it.

But the more I read everything, especially in this section about all things existing within the Dharma realm, I started having an understanding of what it means that they're dependent on causes and conditions, but they don't come into existence from them.
And I remembered my root teacher, Thich Nhat Hanh, talking about this.
He said it's a game of hide and seek.
I thought, what does he mean, hide and seek?
He said, when the conditions are good for something, it appears.
And when the conditions are no longer adequate, it hides, it disappears.
So he never said that things come into being from causes and conditions.
He said that when conditions are right, the things, just like playing hide and seek, appear.
And when conditions are not right, they hide.
And so I understood that all things are already in existence.
All things are in the Dharma realm.
In my mind I had this insight: in that way of playing hide and seek, all things already exist.
So when causes and conditions are right, it's not that they are created, it's just that they appear.
Because all things are already in existence, all things are already in the Dharma realm.
Anyway, I just wanted to say that because at first it was puzzling to me, but I feel like I have a deeper understanding of it now, especially when I related it to what Thich Nhat Hanh was saying.
Kim, do you have a question?

You can let me know.

*Purna, you have also asked how it is that the primary elements, earth, water, fire and wind, are in their fundamental natures completely interfused with each other everywhere throughout the Dharma realm.*
*You wonder how it is that the primary elements, water and fire, do not overcome each other in mutual annihilation.
You also asked, why is it that the primary elements, space and earth, can both exist everywhere throughout the Dharma realm, while being incompatible with each other?
Consider, Purna, that the essential attribute of space is the absence of anything else.
Still, that does not prevent anything else from appearing within it.
How can that be, Purna?
The sky is bright when the sun shines.
It darkens when the clouds gather.*
*There's a movement through when the wind blows.
After a rain, the sun reappears and the air is clear.
Do these various conditioned phenomena appear in different circumstances and come into being because of these conditions?
Or do they come into being because of space?
Suppose, Purna, that these phenomena arise because of the circumstances mentioned.
Then, for example, when the sun's shining, does the brightness in the air come into being because the sun is shining?
If so, then the sun would be everywhere.
Why do we see it as a distinct round object in the sky?*
*If, on the other hand, the brightness of the sky comes into being because of space, then all the space will be shining of its own accord.
Why is it not resplendent with light at midnight or when there are clouds or fog?
It should be clear to you that brightness in the sky is not due to the sun or space, although the brightness cannot be present without sun or space.
The same is said of the true wondrous understanding, which is enlightenment.
If one develops the category space in one's mind, then space will appear within enlightenment.
Earth, water, fire, and wind each appear within enlightenment if one establishes each of them as a category.
All of them appear interfused together in enlightenment if one establishes the category all.
How can they appear together?*
*It is like the sun's reflection in a body of water when two people who are observing the reflection move apart.
One is to the east and one goes to the west.
They will each see the sun's reflection moving with them.
In itself, the reflection has no location.* This part's funny.
*Do not quibble by asking how a single reflection can move in two separate directions and do not ask how the two reflections appeared previously as one.

Such questions concern mere illusions and nothing about reality can be established from them.* And yet he uses that example, which I liked, about the two people seeing the sun and moving away from each other.
*You should realize that all these phenomena are fundamentally unreal and so one cannot specify anything about them in their fundamental natures.
The primary elements are a single reality, which is simply the wondrous awakened enlightenment, the wondrous awakened enlightened mind.
Within the matrix of the thus come one space and the world of perceived objects are everywhere throughout the Dharma realm.
Being suffocated by their confusion, turn their backs on enlightenment and embrace this world of perceived objects.
Amidst the stress of beings entanglement with perceived objects, the world of conditioned phenomena appear.
With my wondrous luminous understanding that neither comes from being nor ceases to be, I am identical to the matrix of the thus come one.
The matrix of the thus come one is itself the wondrous enlightened luminous understanding, which illuminated the entire Dharma realm.
Within it, therefore, the one is infinitely many and the infinitely many are one.*
*The great appears within the small just as the small appear within the great.
I sit unmoving in this still place for awakening and my Dharma body extends everywhere and encompasses the infinity of space in all ten directions.
On the tip of a fine hair, magnificent Buddha lands appear.
Seated within each mote of dust, I turn the great wheel of Dharma.* So now I have some sense that the small appear in the great and the great in the small and on the tip of a hair.
To me, it feels like all of that is because all things exist within the Dharma realm, and big, small, whatever, it doesn't really have, it's kind of beyond that or something.
*Because I have freed myself from the world of perceived objects, I have become one with enlightenment.*

*Therefore, the suchness of reality manifests the inherent nature that is wondrous, luminous, and awake.* He says, *the matrix of the thus come one, the fundamental perfect mind is not the distinction making mind, nor is it space, nor earth, nor the eye faculty, nor visible objects, nor sounds, nor consciousness, neither old age and death, nor precepts or patience or wisdom, etc.* And then there's a commentary here that says, *if you can understand that within the Buddha's realm, there is no is and no is not, you can become enlightened.
The paragraph above just spoke of the emptiness of the matrix.

And now the Buddha will show that this emptiness is not empty.* So then the Buddha continues, *yet it is the distinction making mind, it is space, it is earth, it is the eye faculty and visible objects, sounds, consciousness, old age and death, precepts, patience, wisdom, etc.
It is everything including the thus come one, it is the permanence, bliss, true self and purity of the great nirvana.
It is every one of these, be they mundane or world transcending, that is the wondrousness of the inherent luminous mind that understands.*
*It is apart from is and is not, yet both is and is not.* So that was chapter three.
So chapter four, I'm going to do a quick little dive into chapter four.
It's called Delusion Has No Basis, the parable of Yajnadatta.
And I think Chris may continue with this.
No?

So Purnas says that there was a time when he was plagued with the deluded acts of mind and for a long time bound to the cycle of death and rebirth, and asked, why do all beings suffer from delusion?
The Buddha states, *you have put your coarser doubts, excuse me, to rest, but your more subtle doubts have not yet ended.
Have you heard of Yajnadatta, the man from Shravasti who saw a face with perfectly clear features in the mirror and became enraptured with it?
Then he became upset because he supposed he had lost his face.
It struck him that he had become a headless ghost for no reason.*
*He ran madly out of his house.
What do you think?
What caused this man to run madly about for no good reason?
Purnas replied, he was clearly insane.
That and nothing else was the cause.
The Buddha said, the luminous understanding of wondrous enlightenment is perfect.
How could there be in it any basis for what is clearly delusion?
Thus, your diluted thoughts have followed one upon another, each one leading to the next.*
*Confusion is added to confusion, eon after countless eon, numberless as motes of dust.
Although the Buddha can reveal this process for you, he cannot reverse it for you.
Therefore, beings are not aware of the cause of their confusion because they do not realize that confusion is based upon confusion, their confusion persists.

They need merely to realize that confusion has no ultimate basis and the basis of their diluted thoughts will disappear.* So I think about generational karma a lot, like how one misperception from one ancestor leads to the misperception in the next children, the next generation and so on.
*All that is needed for you is not to follow after the discrimination, after the distinctions you make concerning perpetuations.*

Thich Nhat Hanh always talks about how everything and everyone is made of non-self elements.
